core: What tertiary prevention is: actions that reduce harm and improve quality of life after disease or injury has occurred (WHO Health Promotion Glossary working definition, attributed)
The idea: limit disability and prevent further decline, with an original example
The tools: rehabilitation, support programs, and managing complications, each with one line and an original example
Tertiary prevention versus the other levels: late stage (established condition) vs before onset vs early stage
Who does it: rehabilitation teams, care programs, and communities, each named with one line
The honest note: tertiary prevention is the safety net
The honest framing: tertiary prevention turns surviving into living

claims.claim: Tertiary prevention is the level of prevention that acts after disease or injury has occurred: the WHO Health Promotion Glossary of Terms (2021) describes it as aiming to soften the impact of an ongoing illness or injury that has lasting effects, helping people manage long-term, often-complex health problems to improve their ability to function, their quality of life, and their life expectancy.

The idea of tertiary prevention is to limit disability and prevent further decline: the WHO glossary describes tertiary prevention as managing an established illness or injury to avoid deterioration and complications, naming rehabilitation as the example.

Rehabilitation is a set of interventions designed to optimize functioning and reduce disability in individuals with health conditions in interaction with their environment; it helps a child, adult, or older person be as independent as possible in everyday activities and enables participation in education, work, recreation, and meaningful life roles (WHO Rehabilitation fact sheet, 22 April 2024).

The rehabilitation workforce is made up of different health workers, including physiotherapists, occupational therapists, speech and language therapists, audiologists, orthotists and prosthetists, and clinical psychologists.

Rehabilitation can be provided in many places: inpatient or outpatient hospital settings, outpatient physiotherapy or occupational therapy practices, and community settings such as a person's home, a school, or a workplace.
Rehabilitation is an essential part of universal health coverage, alongside promotion of good health, prevention of disease, treatment, and palliative care.

The three levels of prevention act at different moments of a health problem: primary prevention before onset, secondary prevention in the early (silent) stage, and tertiary prevention after the disease or injury is established and lasting; the WHO glossary treats the levels as complementary measures along the course of disease.
Secondary prevention, the sibling level, works through early detection: screening tests look for diseases before you have symptoms, when they are easier to treat (MedlinePlus Health Screening).

conflictingEvidence.issue: Tertiary prevention is sometimes described as overlapping with treatment or palliative care, and some popular framings restrict 'prevention' to stopping disease before it starts.
positions: Some popular descriptions treat prevention as only primary prevention (stopping disease before onset), leaving tertiary work to be labeled simply 'treatment'.

The WHO Health Promotion Glossary treats prevention as covering measures that reduce the occurrence of risk factors, prevent the occurrence of disease, arrest its progress, and reduce its consequences once established, so tertiary prevention (reducing consequences of an established condition) is squarely inside prevention.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: This lesson follows the WHO glossary framing: tertiary prevention is a named level of prevention concerned with limiting harm and protecting function and quality of life after disease or injury is established, with rehabilitation as its canonical example.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The machine-generated draft's claim that tertiary prevention is 'a foundational concept in Public Health' with no definition, mechanism, or attribution was discarded as boilerplate; the lesson instead teaches the attributed WHO working definition.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the generic draft text with a source-verified lesson: the working definition is attributed to the WHO Health Promotion Glossary of Terms (2021); the tools, workforce, and settings of rehabilitation follow the WHO Rehabilitation fact sheet; the secondary-prevention contrast follows MedlinePlus Health Screening.

sourceRecords.notes: Reused registry id with identical URL. sourceRecords.title: Rehabilitation (fact sheet)
sourceRecords.notes: Fetched and read directly 2026-08-22 (fact sheet dated 22 April 2024). Supports: the working definition of rehabilitation (a set of interventions designed to optimize functioning and reduce disability in individuals with health conditions in interaction with their environment); that rehabilitation helps people be as independent as possible in everyday activities and enables participation in education, work, recreation, and meaningful life roles; that the workforce includes physiotherapists, occupational therapists, speech and language therapists, audiologists, orthotists and prosthetists, and clinical psychologists; that rehabilitation is provided in inpatient/outpatient hospital settings and community settings such as home, school, or workplace; and that rehabilitation is an essential part of universal health coverage alongside promotion, prevention, treatment, and palliative care. WHO-copyrighted fact sheet; facts restated in original prose, no wording reproduced.
